overview: This imported label covers changing kingdoms in and around Upper Myanmar between 1492 and 1650. It includes the rise of Toungoo power, but the outline leaves southern Pegu separately labelled and cannot display Bayinnaung’s far larger empire. Pegu examples below explain the northern kingdoms’ imperial connections beyond the shading. Regional rivals, a vast sixteenth-century empire and a smaller restored kingdom followed one another; 1492 and 1650 are map seams, not founding and extinction dates.

periods.title: Regional kingdoms and Toungoo’s rise
periods.summary: The Irrawaddy basin contained competing political centres before Toungoo’s great expansion.

periods.title: Expansion and fragmentation
periods.summary: Toungoo rulers extended power across the basin and into neighbouring Tai realms; the imperial system then fractured.

periods.title: Restoration on a smaller scale
periods.summary: A restored dynasty consolidated a more compact realm, with its centre returning to Ava.

items.text: Toungoo grew from a regional power into an empire reaching far beyond the Irrawaddy valley. Conquered Tai kingdoms on both sides of the Salween entered its political orbit. Its reach extended from Manipur in the west to Sipsong Panna and Laos in the east.

Tabinshwehti conquered Pegu in 1539 and moved his capital there. Burmese, Mon and Shan people participated in the resulting court and administration. He married a Mon queen and adopted a Mon hairstyle: royal identity could be deliberately mixed, even amid violent conquest.

Royal edicts studied by Toru Ohno describe a palace divided by brick walls. Administrative rooms lay east; queens, princesses and women servants occupied the western household. Movement between these areas was restricted. A palace was both a seat of government and a large, carefully controlled place of work and residence.

Government needed skilled readers and writers. Chief secretaries recorded council decisions for submission to the king through the privy council. Royal orders were written down and relayed through royal reporters to the council. The edicts let us follow this paperwork trail without assuming that every subject could read.

Bayinnaung donated a bronze bell at Shwezigon in Bagan on 23 May 1557. Its inscription has 43 lines in Burmese, 35 in Mon and five in Pali. The same object brought royal commemoration, Buddhist devotion and several written languages together; it survives at the pagoda.

The bell is about 165 centimetres high, with two hamsa birds decorating its hanging hook. Its text recounts victories and religious works. Read it as a king’s public account of his reign: a beautifully made bronze monument can also be a political argument.

Excavation of Kanbawzathadi Palace in Bago began in 1991 and continued into 1997. Archaeologists recovered burnt teak posts, brick remains and religious objects. Some posts carry sixteenth-century inscriptions naming court officers. The report distinguishes possible Bayinnaung-era remains from later building work.

The striking palace buildings now seen at the site are reconstructions informed by archaeology, historical descriptions and traditional craftsmanship. Burnt posts are displayed beside them. Comparing the surviving wood with the reconstructed halls is a useful detective exercise: which parts are evidence, and which show an informed attempt to rebuild?

Elizabeth Howard Moore identifies a roughly 571-hectare walled and moated sixteenth-century Bago, beside an older settlement. Researchers compared a 1942 aerial photograph with a 2002 satellite image to trace features such as walls and the palace area. Sometimes a city’s buried plan becomes clearer from above.

A chronicle examined by U Thaw Kaung describes Bayinnaung standardizing trading weights shaped like hamsa ducks. It also lists port imports including cloth, perfume, spices and colourful parrots. Buying and selling could involve a metal bird on the scales and a live bird among the cargo!

Ralph Fitch’s published account of his late-1580s journey describes families living aboard riverboats and markets held on the water. Boat traders sheltered beneath broad umbrellas made from leaves, compared to cartwheels. Your shop, transport and home could share one hull.

The same account describes merchants’ bamboo houses with straw roofs in old Pegu. Brick storerooms protected goods when fires swept through the flammable neighbourhood. A warehouse could be a household’s most important fire precaution.

Fitch’s account also describes water jars at temple entrances for washing feet. Monks collected rice, fish and herbs in covered pots, receiving food from households along their route. People also gathered to hear monks preach, connecting religious teaching with household giving. These are an outsider’s descriptions of local practices.

A law report set at Bayinnaung’s court tells of a Tai noble family disputing inheritance. An elder son had entered royal service. Was money previously given to him support while he served, or his inheritance paid early? Judge Kyaw Thu ruled in his favour, interpreting the family’s obligations and intentions. The surviving text reaches us through much later copies.

A short Burmese sample, in Huxley’s scholarly Roman transliteration, is “Shin kyaw thu pyatton”, translated “Lord Kyaw Thu’s Precedent”. It names the inheritance report preserved in an 1870 printed edition. This is a later witness to a text about the sixteenth-century court, not a surviving sixteenth-century autograph; the Roman letters represent Burmese words rather than reproducing Burmese script.

Fitch’s published account describes petitions written on long strips of leaves with a pointed iron stylus and submitted to the king. Important writing did not have to begin with a sheet of paper: a prepared leaf could carry a request to court.

In the 1590s, unsuccessful warfare in Siam and demands for service and taxes helped break the empire apart. The restored dynasty built a smaller Irrawaddy-centred kingdom, curtailed princely autonomy and used appointed governors. Its rulers sought more manageable government instead of recovering every distant dependency.

ending.text: The map stops in 1650, but the restored Toungoo dynasty continued until Pegu’s conquest of Upper Myanmar in 1752. Alaungpaya then led the movement that established the Konbaung dynasty. These were changes of ruling institutions; the region’s households, languages, trade and Buddhist traditions did not disappear at the map seam.
